confidence_note: The '1-3-5 rule' (one big, three medium, five small tasks) in the TR text is a widely circulated productivity technique that could not be attributed to Robin Sharma, and the claim that he studied leaders' morning routines and found this pattern, plus the quote about 9 versus 50 tasks, could not be verified. They are excluded. The closest verified idea in The 5AM Club (the assumed source; its usual Turkish title differs from the input) is the 'Daily 5': each morning, write down five small targets you want to achieve that day, which the book says adds up to 1,825 small wins over a year. The facts below describe that concept. The writer should consider whether this story needs replacing, as it no longer matches the TR text.
facts: In The 5AM Club, Sharma proposes the 'Daily 5': each morning, list five small goals you want to complete that day.
The book's arithmetic is that five small wins a day adds up to 1,825 over a year, presented as an illustration of compounding, not as a measured outcome.
The idea is to decide in the morning what the day's small victories will be, rather than letting incoming demands decide.
It fits the book's broader theme of protecting a morning block for planning and focus before the day's distractions begin.
tension: Writing down only five small targets seems too modest to matter, yet the book's point is that a short, clear list chosen in advance adds up where a vague intention does not.
opening_idea: Begin with someone writing just five small targets on a card at dawn, and ask what that short list can do that a long list cannot.

lessons.idea: A short list chosen in the morning puts your priorities ahead of the day's interruptions.
Small daily wins add up to something large only over a long time, which the book shows with simple arithmetic.
lessons.anchor: Five a day becomes 1,825 in a year.

reflect: At the end of an ordinary day, how many of the things you did were ones you chose yourself?
What would be on your list if it could only hold five small items?
reflect_final: Tomorrow morning, write down five small things you want to finish that day and check them in the evening. Notice whether the short list changed what you did first.

use_cases.situation: Your to-do list has grown so long that you start each day not knowing what to do first.
use_cases.move: Borrow Sharma's Daily 5: before opening email, pick just five small items for today and set the rest aside.

use_cases.situation: A team's daily stand-up lists far more work than anyone can finish.
use_cases.move: Suggest each person names at most five concrete things they will finish today, and review them the next day.

use_cases.situation: A direct report feels overwhelmed and unproductive despite long hours.
use_cases.move: Ask them to name five small things they could finish today, then check in at the end of the day on which ones got done.

pocket_idea: Five small targets written at dawn: a short list you chose beats a long one the day chooses for you.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Robin Sharma counts five small wins a day as 1,825 in a year.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In The 5AM Club, Sharma asks readers to write five small goals every morning, arguing that deciding the day's small victories first, before other demands, adds up to 1,825 of them a year.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Ask how many items are on their to-do list right now, and which five they would keep if they could only keep five.
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: A long list the day fills for you versus five targets you choose in the morning.
